newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl, Clinton renew friendship over dinner.
newsitem.headline: Kohl, Clinton renew friendship over dinner.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and President Bill Clinton held wide-ranging discussions and renewed their friendship during a lengthy working dinner at a posh Georgetown restaurant on Wednesday.
Kohl arrived in Washington for a one-day trip to attend ceremonies on Thursday marking the 50th anniversary of the Marshall Plan, and squeezed in a three-hour dinner with Clinton.
White House spokeswoman Anne Luzzatto described the mood as jovial, and said the evening's talks -- held through interpreters -- were interspersed with storytelling and jokes.

"These are two men who like each other very much," Luzzatto said after Clinton and Kohl retired for the evening. They will meet again in two weeks at the Denver summit of the Group of Seven industrialised nations.
Topics discussed included the European Union, the British and French elections, the German economy and ways to balance economic growth with safety net needs, she said.
Kohl, facing mounting scepticism over whether Germany can qualify for European monetary union, underscored his deep personal commitment to European integration during the talks.
"As a child of war, Kohl is very much a European integrationist," Luzzatto said.

Clinton and Kohl also discussed NATO expansion, the G7 summit, Bosnia and the need to push along reconstruction efforts there, as well as Turkey and the expansion of the European Union, Russia and the importance of arms reductions, as well as the election of a moderate government in Iran.

Kohl's government was forced this week to back down from a confrontation with the Bundesbank over a plan to revalue the central bank's gold reserves and transfer the profits to help reduce German debt and help German qualify for EMU.
Asked to comment on Kohl's EMU difficulties, Clinton said, "Well they're just challenges."
He also underscored the importance of U.S-German ties, especially in light of NATO expansion and European integration.
The two men, renowned for their hearty appetites, took a much more moderate approach to the menu than on their last visit to the same restaurant a few years ago.

Clinton started his meal with venison crostinin a red pepper sauce and minestrone, and ate zitti primavera and smoked chicken ravioli. Kohl began with a tomato mozzarella salad and minestrone, choosing grilled salmon as his main course. Both men skipped dessert, despite a sumptious display of tortes, tiramisu and other Italian pastries.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry last week predicted as much, noting Clinton was on a diet and Kohl faced an election campaign.
National Security Advisor Samuel Berger and his German counterpart Joachim Bitterlich also attended the dinner.
Kohl was due to attend a wreath-laying on Thursday morning and go to an evening gala to commemorate the work of former Secretary of State George Marshall.
Under the Marshall plan, which he briefly outlined in a speech at Harvard University on June 5, 1947, the United States provided billions of dollars in aid to rebuild Europe after World War Two.
